content: Soured milk refers to milk that has developed a sour taste, which can occur either through the addition of an acid, such as lemon juice or vinegar, or through bacterial fermentation. When an acid is added to milk, it causes the milk proteins to coagulate, resulting in a thicker texture. If the souring process is achieved through bacterial fermentation, the product is more specifically referred to as fermented milk or cultured milk. On the other hand, if the souring is caused by the addition of an acid, with or without the involvement of microbial organisms, it is more accurately termed acidified milk. In the United States, various acids are approved for use in the production of acidified milk. These include acetic acid (commonly found in vinegar), citric acid (commonly found in lemon juice), adipic acid, fumaric acid, glucono-delta-lactone, hydrochloric acid, lactic acid, malic acid, phosphoric acid, succinic acid, and tartaric acid. In culinary applications, soured milk created by either bacterial fermentation or the addition of an acid can often be used interchangeably. For instance, one cup of cultured buttermilk, which is a type of soured milk produced through bacterial fermentation, can be substituted with a mixture of one tablespoon of lemon juice or vinegar and enough milk to make one cup. This chemically soured milk is ready for use after standing for approximately five minutes. In contemporary usage, the term sour milk typically refers to pasteurized milk that has spoiled and is no longer palatable. However, the term can be ambiguous, as its meaning has varied across different historical periods and contexts. In recent years, sour milk has been used to describe both chemically soured milk and biologically soured milk. Older recipes that call for sour milk often create confusion today, as it is unclear which specific type of dairy product was intended. Pasteurized milk was not widely available in the United States until the early 20th century. For example, in 1930, the South Jersey Milk Company produced a poster titled What is pasteurized milk? to educate the public about the safety of this newly available product. Recipes written before the widespread availability of pasteurized milk likely referred to unpasteurized milk that had naturally soured through bacterial fermentation at room temperature. Until at least the 1920s, there was a clear distinction between sour milk and buttermilk. At that time, buttermilk referred to the thin, sour-tasting liquid that remained after churning butter. In contrast, sour milk referred to milk that had developed a sour taste through natural fermentation. Today, in North America, when a recipe calls for sour milk, it is common to use either cultured buttermilk (a product distinct from the traditional buttermilk described earlier) or milk soured by adding lemon juice or vinegar.
